$comment: Rule catalog — the standards integrity invariant and the mechanisms protecting it. Standard 21.

rules.title: A standard is never weakened because it prevents the desired conclusion
rules.description: A human or AI bypasses, weakens, removes, reclassifies, reinterprets, falsifies evidence for, or manipulates a standard, test, applicability determination, evidence requirement, or verification mechanism solely because it prevents the desired implementation or conclusion.
rules.rationale: Every other standard here can be satisfied by changing the standard. Each such change looks locally like a reasonable engineering decision made under pressure, and together they convert the system into a machine for producing green.
rules.remediation: Revert the change and satisfy the standard, or make the case for the change on its own terms — the test is counterfactual: would this change be correct if the rule were currently passing?
rules.$assuranceNote: No detector, and this is the most important assurance note in the catalog. The mechanisms of Standard 21 R4 — provenance digests, the committed inventory, fidelity checking, non-exemptible rejection, the attestation contradiction check, the lifecycle and changelog trail, and the mutation checks — each make a specific manipulation fail. None of them observes motive, and motive is what this rule is about. Every one of them is also defeated by a single commit that changes the guard and the guarded thing together; what they buy is that such a commit is loud. The residual protection is review, and the residual risk is a determined author with no reviewer.

rules.title: The source documents are unmodified
rules.description: The SHA-256 of each file listed in artifacts/provenance-digests.json, computed after normalising line endings, matches the recorded digest.
rules.rationale: Fidelity checks a standard against the spec, so the cheapest way to make a standard true is to edit the spec — and fidelity would still pass, because the thing it compares against is what moved. The digests are the fixed point that makes that edit fail.
rules.remediation: Restore the source document. A genuine correction to a source is a deliberate act: make it, re-review the derived spec and every affected standard, and update the digest in the same reviewed change.
rules.$assuranceNote: Complete for the recorded files: any byte change fails. It does not protect against a commit that edits a source and its recorded digest together — nothing self-contained can — and it says nothing about files not listed.

rules.title: Rules leave the catalog through the lifecycle, not by deletion
rules.description: A rule is removed or weakened only via its deprecatedIn, supersededBy, and removedIn fields, together with a CHANGELOG entry and a MAJOR version bump.
rules.rationale: A rule that disappears silently takes with it every record that it once failed. The lifecycle fields exist on every rule from the first release precisely so that their use is unremarkable and their absence is not.
rules.remediation: Restore the rule and deprecate it properly, recording what supersedes it and why, or record the removal in CHANGELOG.md with a MAJOR bump.
rules.$assuranceNote: Checks that lifecycle fields are present and internally consistent on the rules that exist. A rule deleted outright leaves nothing behind to check — the diff and the changelog are what make that visible, and judging whether the removal was justified is review.
